name: Double cleansing

lead: Double cleansing means washing the face twice in the evening: first with an oil, balm or micellar water, then with a water-based cleanser. It comes from Korean and Japanese beauty routines.
Proponents say it removes sunscreen, makeup and sebum more completely than a single wash. No published trial has tested the routine itself.

paras: The oil step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as sunscreen and sebum; the water-based step then removes what remains and rinses the oil away.
Risks are mild and mainly relate to irritation from over-washing and, for some people, breakouts from comedogenic oils. Evidence for cleansing practices in general is described as limited.

lead: Double cleansing is a two-step facial washing routine in which an oil-based or other lipid-soluble cleanser (a cleansing oil, balm or micellar water) is applied first, followed by a water-based cleanser that is emulsified with water and rinsed off.[1] It is associated with Korean and Japanese beauty routines and is described in looksmaxxing and skincare communities as an evening step used to remove sunscreen, makeup and sebum.[1][2]

Proponents say the first step dissolves oil-soluble residues such as water-resistant sunscreen and waterproof makeup that a single water-based wash may leave behind, and that the second step removes the remaining oil and water-soluble debris.[1] Dermatologists quoted in general references describe cleansing as a routine part of acne care but note that evidence for specific cleansing practices is limited.[3] No published clinical trial has tested double cleansing as a regimen for acne or appearance.
infobox: None found for the routine itself

paras: In the commonly described form, a lipid-soluble cleanser such as a cleansing oil, balm or micellar water is massaged onto dry skin, the face may be splashed with water, and a water-based cleanser is then lathered or emulsified and rinsed off thoroughly.[1] The first step is intended for residues that resist water, including water-resistant sunscreen, long-wear makeup, excess sebum and particulate pollution.[1]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and skincare communities
paras: In style- and skin-focused communities it is typically presented as an evening routine layered with other steps (toner, actives, moisturiser), and is often discussed alongside the oil cleansing method and skin cycling. Practitioners usually describe it as a way to keep skin clear of sunscreen and sebum build-up without relying on a single harsh wash.

General references on facial cleansers state that cleansing can help remove oil and debris and that many cleanser claims, such as effects on pore clogging or oil production, are insufficiently sourced.[1] A broader skincare overview notes that evidence for best cleansing practices is limited.[3]
A questionnaire study of 539 Korean patients with acne examined how cosmetics use relates to acne, but it did not test double cleansing as an intervention.[4]

Reported concerns are generally the same as for any cleansing: over-washing or aggressive scrubbing can irritate skin and impair the skin barrier, and some oils used in the first step are described by dermatologists as potentially comedogenic for some people.[3][2]

No studies found. The routine itself has not been tested in published trials; research is limited to broader work on cosmetics use and acne, such as an observational questionnaire study in Korean acne patients.[4]

lore.intro: Double cleansing is discussed in skincare-adjacent looksmaxxing spaces as a standard evening routine, usually without controlled evidence either way.[1]

claims.claim: Cleansing twice, oil first, removes sunscreen and sebum that one wash leaves behind.
Double cleansing keeps pores clear and helps acne-prone skin.
